text: Hands-on lab: take a single tangled does-everything function and refactor it through every layer this chapter built — separated construction and execution, a backend interface, and a decision about an optional SDK-adapter boundary — then verify the refactor didn't change behavior.

This lesson covers a full refactor walkthrough on one realistic function, how to verify a refactor is behavior-preserving using the statevector technique from Chapter 2, where to stop adding abstraction layers for a project that doesn't need multi-SDK support, and a practical architecture review checklist.

Here's the starting point: a function that estimates GHZ-state fidelity, fusing circuit construction, a boolean flag choosing between simulator and real hardware, and the fidelity calculation, all in one function with a print statement thrown in. This single function has every problem the last few lessons warned about: construction and execution fused together, a backend chosen via a boolean flag instead of injection, and no way to test the circuit logic without running a backend.

The refactor splits this into three functions. build_ghz_circuit does pure construction, following lesson ten's principle. run_and_get_counts takes the circuit and an injected backend, following lesson eleven's shared interface. fidelity_from_counts extracts the analysis logic entirely, following the separation principle from Chapter 1. The composed top-level function then takes the backend as a parameter, so calling code chooses it explicitly and uniformly between development and production.

A refactor that changes structure without changing behavior needs proof, not assumption. The real payoff shows up in a test like this one: fidelity_from_counts is now testable with a hand-constructed counts dictionary and zero quantum execution at all — completely impossible in the original tangled function, where fidelity calculation and circuit execution were inseparable.

This refactor deliberately stopped at the backend-abstraction layer and did not add an SDK-adapter layer, because this project only targets Qiskit-compatible backends — adding that abstraction with no second SDK in sight would be exactly the speculative over-engineering last lesson warned against. Before calling any module's architecture done, check: construction, execution, and analysis are separate functions; the backend is always a parameter, never a boolean flag; each extracted function has an independent test; no abstraction layer exists that the project doesn't currently need; and the composed top-level function reads as a short, readable sequence of calls.

That closes Chapter 3's architecture work. Chapter 4 turns to reproducibility — starting with version control practices that make a reported result traceable back to the exact commit that produced it.
